..
Issued at 200 AM CDT Thu Sep 10 2026

Isentropic ascent and a weak passing wave have led to an increase in 
coverage of showers and storms early this morning, primarily south 
of Interstate 70 along the nose of the LLJ. While severe 
weather is unlikely, effective shear of ~20kts along with 1000 
J/kg of elevated instability could lead to a couple of stronger 
storms capable of producing gusty winds. There remains some 
concern for heavy rainfall and localized flooding with PWATs 
around 2" and storm motions parallel to the elevated boundary. 
00z HREF members are less expansive with the 1"+ rainfall 
footprint than yesterday, but still show bands of heavier 
rainfall in the 1-3" range across east-central Kansas. Rainfall 
rates have been as high as 0.5-1.5" per hour so far, which could
lead to these higher amounts in areas impacted by multiple 
rounds of storms. All-in- all, think the dry antecedent 
conditions will keep flooding concerns on the low end, but could
see some localized flooding along and south of Interstate 35.

Precipitation comes to an end this morning and skies clear from 
north to south. A much more comfortable day is expected with highs 
in the 80s. There is a low chance for a pop-up shower or storm this 
afternoon/evening across east-central Kansas as model soundings show 
a weakly capped airmass in place. Forcing is weak and subsidence 
behind this morning's wave should work to suppress convection and 
keep conditions dry. High boundary layer moisture, light surface 
winds, and clear skies create a favorable set-up for fog to develop 
tonight into Friday morning. Have input patchy fog for now, but some 
guidance suggests fog could be more widespread.

Quieter weather builds into the area Friday as mid-level subsidence 
behind the shortwave trough spreads across eastern Kansas. Low-level 
flow returning to the south with mostly clear skies should help to 
return temperatures back into the upper 80s by the mid to late 
afternoon. Rain and storm chances will begin to increase again by 
Friday night and through much of Saturday with the next upper level 
disturbance moving off the central Rockies. Guidance remains
mixed in the development of an MCS Friday evening/night. The
global models and ensembles continue to show the highest chances
of a convective complex forming and potentially impacting the
forecast area, while short-range guidance largely fails to
generate any convection. Will need to monitor trends as any MCS
that does impact the area could bring strong to severe storms.
With scattered precipitation and ample cloud cover for most of 
Saturday, high temps should stay around the mid 80s. 

By Sunday and Monday, a strong PNW upper low will begin to eject 
across the northern Rockies as the southwestern US ridge expands 
west into the southern Plains. Breezy south winds will and
diurnal mixing Sunday and Monday could be offset by clouds and
precipitation. If cloud/precipitation coverage is less, highs
could be back in the 90s for most. 

Relatively cooler temperatures should come again as a frontal 
boundary moves into the area Monday afternoon and evening as 
the PNW upper low lifts across the northern Plains. An 
associated surface trough extending from Minnesota to western 
Kansas should track east across the state through the day 
Monday, increasing storm chances yet again. With better height 
falls well north of the area, the surface boundary is expected 
to stall out somewhere across southern Kansas by Tuesday. 
Scattered storm and rain chances along this stalled boundary  
remain common across much of the area Tuesday and in turn, keep 
temperatures on the cooler side. Long range ensemble guidance 
for temperature spreads Tuesday and beyond are still greater 
than 10 degrees so confidence in how long the cool air sticks 
around is still low. That said, deterministic long range 
guidance is hinting at a stout Arctic low digging out of central
Canada by mid to late next week that could bring some more
fall-like air to the region.
